description:
We are Passionate NASA Girls, a team of ambitious and creative girls passionate about space, science, technology, and innovation. 🚀

We believe that great ideas become powerful solutions when curiosity, teamwork, and creativity come together. Through the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to explore real-world challenges, develop innovative ideas, and create solutions that can make a positive impact on our world.
summary:
FIRA is the name of our web application, designed to help users explore and understand fire hotspot observations using NASA satellite data from MODIS and VIIRS.
 
 NASA satellites collect thousands of hotspot observations, but not every hotspot represents an actual fire. Industrial sources, such as gas flares and factories, can also appear as hotspots. This creates noise in the data and makes it difficult to identify possible fire activity and understand its patterns over time.
 
 FIRA aims to address this problem by processing and filtering satellite observations to help distinguish possible fires from fixed heat sources. It also allows users to explore and compare MODIS and VIIRS observations while keeping their data separate because the two sensors have different characteristics.
 
 The project initially focuses on three regions: Oman, Greece, and the western United States (California, Oregon, and Washington). We chose to start with these regions to focus on data quality and improve the reliability of our results before expanding the platform to more countries in the future.
 
 FIRA directly addresses NASA’s challenge “Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots” by making satellite observations easier to access, explore, and compare. Our goal is to support environmental research and awareness by transforming open NASA data into useful information for local communities.
details:
Every day NASA satellites report thousands of hot spots, but a hot spot is not always a fire. A gas flare or a factory shows up the same way, month after month. FIRA is a website that separates the two, so anyone can read a country's real fire history. 

 

How it works

  • For each country, we download the MODIS and VIIRS detection files from NASA FIRMS and analyze them with our own scripts: we read every detection, clean the data, and turn the result into a record the website can display. FIRA covers three regions: Oman, Greece and the US West Coast (California, Oregon and Washington).
  • We remove fixed heat sources: land and offshore flags, low-confidence points, and any area that stayed hot for four years or more. In Oman, for example, we start with 554,548 raw detections since 2000, and about 93% are removed, leaving 41,341. A stricter setting keeps 17,064. 
  • The user picks a country on a 3D globe built from NASA Blue Marble images, then explores its record by sensor, year, region and day, with a map, timeline, calendar and CSV download. Each fire is described by its date, estimated burned area and duration in days. A risk estimate combines real weather data from NASA POWER, dryness, and the months when fires usually appear in the data.

Technology and feasibility

  • FIRA is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. The data are NASA's free FIRMS files. All three countries use the same file format, so the same pipeline processes each one. We also measure the filter's accuracy by checking how many removed points fall on known industrial sites. 

What makes it different

  • It keeps MODIS and VIIRS apart, because VIIRS has finer pixels and more satellites. Adding them together would show growth that is not real.
  • It is built to tell industrial heat from real fires, the main noise in oil-producing countries, and it shows how many removed points fall on known industrial sites.
  • It is made to be explored: you scroll from space down to the country, in Arabic or English.

Science and technology

  • FIRA removes fixed heat sources such as gas flares and factories, which in Oman made up about 93% of the raw detections. It lets users view MODIS and VIIRS separately or together, so they can compare how the two sensors record the same region over time.

Research

  • Each fire is described by its date, estimated burned area and duration in days, by region. Researchers can study how fire frequency and seasons change year after year, and download the data as a CSV file. FIRA also keeps its own archive of the cleaned record, so the history stays available on our site even if NASA's files change or move.

Communities and agencies

  • People can open their own country and region and read its fire history in Arabic or English, so more people in the region can use it. Environmental agencies and planners can see where and in which months fires usually occur, and plan prevention accordingly. 

The challenge

  • FIRA makes NASA's open satellite data easier to read, shows how much of it comes from real fires, and shows what can be built when anyone is allowed to look.

Where it can go

  • The same pipeline works for any country: download its NASA file, check the filter results, and a new region appears. Starting with Oman, Greece and the US West Coast, FIRA can grow into a shared, open record of fire for the whole world.
